chunks.text: Sir Lucian Ravenscroft gave a small dinner at Ravenscroft House on Saturday, 5 December 1891, intending to announce a large transfer of Brazilian railway shares after the toast. At about half past nine he collapsed and Dr. Whitcombe was summoned. The physician says his illness was caused by something he drank at dinner, and that Sir Lucian will recover. The police believe someone interfered with his loving cup. Each guest remembers the evening a little differently. Establish who was where, and when, and which statements cannot all be true. This case is solved by language, seating and timing alone.
chunks.title: Case introduction: The Poisoned Invitation

chunks.text:
INVITATION CARDS - copies kept by the household.

To Lady Margaret Hartwell (21 Nov.): Sir Lucian Ravenscroft requests the pleasure of your company at dinner on Saturday the fifth of December, at eight o'clock. A matter of business will be announced.
To Mr. Robert Hale (22 Nov.): Sir Lucian Ravenscroft requests the pleasure of your company at dinner on Saturday the fifth of December, at eight o'clock.
To Mr. Edward Mills (2 Dec.): At Sir Lucian's request, Lady Margaret Hartwell writes to ask whether you will dine at Ravenscroft House on Saturday the fifth, in place of Captain Ross, who is indisposed. Dinner is at eight.
chunks.title: Invitation Cards
chunks.author: Sir Lucian Ravenscroft; Lady Margaret Hartwell

chunks.text:
GUEST LIST - kept by Mr. Stokes at the door.

Lady Margaret Hartwell - arrived 8:05 PM (detained by fog).
Mr. Robert Hale - arrived 7:40 PM.
Mr. Edward Mills - arrived 7:50 PM; first visit to the house; a stranger to Sir Lucian, whom he met in the hall.
Household in attendance: Mr. Stokes (butler), Henry Tilling (footman), Susan Clarke (household assistant), Mrs. Brand (cook).
chunks.title: Guest List
chunks.author: Mr. Stokes, butler

chunks.text:
SEATING ARRANGEMENT - the dining table, Ravenscroft House.

The sideboard stands against the east wall, beside the head of the table.
Head of the table: Sir Lucian Ravenscroft.
On his right: Lady Margaret Hartwell.
On his left: Mr. Robert Hale.
Middle of the table, right side: Captain Ross's place (vacant).
Foot of the table: Mr. Edward Mills.
The loving cup is set at the host's place before dinner and carried to him from the sideboard for the toast.

chunks.author: Mr. Stokes, butler

chunks.text:
TELEGRAM (copy obtained from the Charing Cross office).

To J. Dray, Manchester. Sir L. to sign nothing after Saturday. Will see to it personally. - E.M.
chunks.title: A Private Message
chunks.author: Edward Mills to J. Dray, Manchester

chunks.text:
Statement of Lady Margaret Hartwell.

I arrived at half past seven. At about five past nine I saw Mr. Hale carry the loving cup to Sir Lucian for the toast. I was seated some distance from the sideboard. After the toast I went with the ladies to the drawing room. I know nothing more.
chunks.title: Statement of Lady Margaret Hartwell
chunks.author: Lady Margaret Hartwell

chunks.text:
Statement of Robert Hale.

I sat at Sir Lucian's left and never left my chair before the toast. The loving cup was carried to Sir Lucian by the gentleman at the foot of the table, whom I had not met before that evening. I know of no reason for anyone to wish Sir Lucian harm.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Robert Hale
chunks.author: Robert Hale

chunks.text:
Statement of Susan Clarke.

I filled the loving cup at nine and left it on the sideboard to fetch the salver from the kitchen. When I came back at about three minutes past nine, Mr. Mills was at the sideboard. He said he would carry the cup to Sir Lucian as a courtesy, and I let him, because he was a guest.
chunks.title: Statement of Miss Susan Clarke
chunks.author: Susan Clarke

chunks.text:
Statement of Edward Mills.

I sat at the foot of the table from the soup until the toast. I never rose from my chair until Sir Lucian was taken ill, and I did not go near the sideboard or touch the cup. I am a stranger in this house and know of no reason why anyone should have wished Sir Lucian harm.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Edward Mills
chunks.author: Edward Mills

chunks.text: Lady Margaret Hartwell, Sir Lucian's business associate. Background: A widow who co-owns a railway syndicate with Sir Lucian. Dignified, grand in manner, fond of being right and prone to small social untruths. Motive: Sir Lucian planned to transfer the Brazilian shares away from her syndicate. Relationship: Business associate of Sir Lucian; she arranged Mr. Mills's invitation. Known whereabouts: Says she arrived at half past seven; went with the ladies to the drawing room after the toast.
chunks.title: Profile of Lady Margaret Hartwell

chunks.text: Personality: Haughty, gossipy, quick to attribute blame, protective of her dignity. She arrived at five past eight, not half past seven, because of fog, and is embarrassed about it. She wrote the invitation to Mr. Mills in Sir Lucian's name. She thought she saw Mr. Hale carry the cup, but she sat far from the sideboard and mistook one gentleman for another. Does not know: Which gentleman actually carried the cup.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Lady Margaret Hartwell

chunks.text: Questions: When did you arrive? Why did you say half past seven? What time did you reach the house? Answer: At half past seven, as I recall. The fog was dreadful, so perhaps it was a little later. I did not consult my watch.
chunks.title: Lady Margaret Hartwell on: When did you arrive

chunks.text: Questions: Who carried the cup to Sir Lucian? Who took the loving cup? Did you see who carried the cup? Answer: I saw a gentleman carry the cup to Sir Lucian at about five past nine. I took it to be Mr. Hale, but I confess I was seated some distance away.
chunks.title: Lady Margaret Hartwell on: Who carried the cup to Sir Lucian

chunks.text: Questions: Why did you invite Mr. Mills? Who is Edward Mills? Why did you write his invitation? Answer: Captain Ross was indisposed and Sir Lucian asked me to find a gentleman to fill the place. Mr. Mills was recommended by my solicitor. I wrote the card on Sir Lucian's behalf.
chunks.title: Lady Margaret Hartwell on: Why did you invite Mr. Mills

chunks.text: Questions: Do you have a motive? Were the shares to be taken from you? Did you quarrel with Sir Lucian? Answer: Sir Lucian intended an announcement about the Brazilian shares. I was displeased, naturally. But I am a lady and I went with the ladies to the drawing room.
chunks.title: Lady Margaret Hartwell on: Do you have a motive

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Mr. Hale, Susan or Mr. Mills? Answer: I would not slander anyone. Mr. Hale has debts; the girl is only a servant; Mr. Mills is a stranger to me.
chunks.title: Lady Margaret Hartwell on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Robert Hale, a family friend. Background: An old friend of Sir Lucian's late brother, who gambles and borrows. Charming, vague about money and apt to change the subject. Motive: Owes Sir Lucian eight hundred pounds, repayable on demand. Relationship: Family friend of Sir Lucian. Known whereabouts: Seated at Sir Lucian's left; says he did not leave his chair before the toast.
chunks.title: Profile of Robert Hale

chunks.text: Personality: Easygoing on the surface, uneasy when asked about money, observant of other guests. He remained in his chair until the toast. He saw the gentleman at the foot of the table rise at about two minutes past nine, go to the sideboard and carry the cup to Sir Lucian. He did not know the gentleman's name; he had not met him before that evening. Does not know: Mr. Mills's name until the introductions at the table.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Robert Hale

chunks.text: Questions: Did you leave your chair before the toast? Where were you at five past nine? Did you go to the sideboard? Answer: I never left my chair before the toast. I sat at Sir Lucian's left throughout. You may ask Tilling the footman.
chunks.title: Robert Hale on: Did you leave your chair before the toast

chunks.text: Questions: Who carried the cup to Sir Lucian? Did you carry the cup? Who took the cup from the sideboard? Answer: Not I. The gentleman at the foot of the table rose and carried it to Sir Lucian. I had not met him before that evening.
chunks.title: Robert Hale on: Who carried the cup to Sir Lucian

chunks.text: Questions: Do you owe Sir Lucian money? Do you have a motive? Why would you want him harmed? Answer: I owe him a sum, and he is the kind of friend who does not call it in. I should be the last man to wish him harm.
chunks.title: Robert Hale on: Do you owe Sir Lucian money

chunks.text: Questions: Who sat at the foot of the table? Who is the gentleman at the foot? Who is Mr. Mills? Answer: Mr. Mills sat at the foot, by the plan. A stranger to me, a Manchester man. Lady Margaret introduced him.
chunks.title: Robert Hale on: Who sat at the foot of the table

chunks.text: Questions: Why does Lady Margaret say you carried the cup? Why do your accounts differ? Answer: Lady Margaret sits at the far side and has poor eyes for faces across a table. She has mistaken one gentleman for another.
chunks.title: Robert Hale on: Why does Lady Margaret say you carried the cup

chunks.text: Susan Clarke, the household assistant. Background: Household assistant to Sir Lucian for three years, trusted with the loving cup and the dinner service. Nervous, honest and afraid of being blamed. Motive: None known; she lives in terror of dismissal. Relationship: Servant of Sir Lucian. Known whereabouts: Filled the loving cup at nine, then went to the kitchen to fetch the salver; back at about three minutes past.
chunks.title: Profile of Susan Clarke

chunks.text: Personality: Anxious, over-eager to please, repeats detail when frightened, never lies but forgets small things. She polished the loving cup at five to nine and filled it at nine. She left it on the sideboard to fetch the salver from the kitchen. When she returned at 9:03 the gentleman from the foot of the table was at the sideboard and said he would carry the cup as a courtesy; she let him, because he was a guest. Does not know: What was done to the cup.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Susan Clarke

chunks.text: Questions: What did you do with the cup? When did you fill the cup? Where was the cup at nine? Answer: I polished it at five to nine and filled it at nine. I left it on the sideboard and went to the kitchen to fetch the salver, sir.
chunks.title: Susan Clarke on: What did you do with the cup

chunks.text: Questions: Who carried the cup? Who took the cup from the sideboard? Who was at the sideboard? Answer: When I came back at about three minutes past nine, Mr. Mills was at the sideboard. He said he would carry the cup to Sir Lucian as a courtesy, and I let him, sir, because he was a guest.
chunks.title: Susan Clarke on: Who carried the cup

chunks.text: Questions: Did you go near the cup after nine? Were you in the dining room? Did you leave the cup? Answer: Only to fetch the salver, sir, and I was in the kitchen when Cook can say. Three minutes, no more.
chunks.title: Susan Clarke on: Did you go near the cup after nine

chunks.text: Questions: Who is Mr. Mills? Did you know him? Had you seen him before? Answer: He is the gentleman who sat at the foot of the table. I had not seen him before that evening.
chunks.title: Susan Clarke on: Who is Mr. Mills

chunks.text: Questions: Why were you alone with the cup? Who else came near? Why did nobody watch? Answer: The cup is always left on the sideboard until the toast, sir. Nobody would think to watch it.
chunks.title: Susan Clarke on: Why were you alone with the cup

chunks.text: Edward Mills, a visiting guest. Background: A Manchester financier who joined the dinner at the last moment in place of Captain Ross. Affable, ambitious, and a member of a syndicate that stands to profit from Sir Lucian's refusal to sign. Motive: His syndicate would profit if Sir Lucian were prevented from signing the Brazilian transfer. Relationship: Visiting guest, a stranger to Sir Lucian, invited through Lady Margaret. Known whereabouts: Seated at the foot of the table; claims he never rose or went near the sideboard.
chunks.title: Profile of Edward Mills

chunks.text: Personality: Smooth, polite, quick with a joke, answers evasively and with apparent candour. SECRET (never admit): at 9:02 he rose from the foot of the table, went to the sideboard and offered to carry the cup, then carried it to Sir Lucian at the toast. He sent a telegram to a Manchester associate that said Sir Lucian would sign nothing after Saturday. He never confesses; he denies going near the sideboard. Does not know: That the footman noted him rising.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Edward Mills

chunks.text: Questions: Did you go near the sideboard? Did you rise from your seat? Did you touch the cup? Answer: I never rose from my chair until Sir Lucian fell ill. I did not go near the sideboard and I did not touch the cup.
chunks.title: Edward Mills on: Did you go near the sideboard

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you sitting? Which seat was yours? Who sat at the foot of the table? Answer: I sat at the foot of the table, as the plan will show. Far from the host, as you can see, and far from any sideboard.
chunks.title: Edward Mills on: Where were you sitting

chunks.text: Questions: Who carried the cup to Sir Lucian? Why does Susan say you carried the cup? Why does the footman say a gentleman rose? Answer: Susan is a frightened girl and Tilling is a footman. They may be thinking of another gentleman. I remained in my chair.
chunks.title: Edward Mills on: Who carried the cup to Sir Lucian

chunks.text: Questions: What does your telegram mean? Why did you send a message about Sir Lucian signing nothing? What did you mean? Answer: I meant what a man of business means, Inspector. That the matter would be settled, one way or the other. It was a figure of speech.
chunks.title: Edward Mills on: What does your telegram mean

chunks.text: Questions: Why were you invited? Do you have a motive? Does your syndicate gain? Answer: I was invited to fill a vacancy. As for my syndicate, it has an interest in the shares like any other. That is not a crime.
chunks.title: Edward Mills on: Why were you invited

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Lady Margaret or Mr. Hale? Answer: Lady Margaret is out of sorts when thwarted, and Mr. Hale is a man in debt. I should not like to say more.
chunks.title: Edward Mills on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Consider opportunity. The cup was filled at nine and the toast was at five past. Who handled the cup in those five minutes, and who says they did not?"
chunks.title: Watson hint 1

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "People describe one another differently: 'Mr. Hale' to Lady Margaret, 'the gentleman at the foot of the table' to Mr. Hale and the footman. Use the seating arrangement to learn who sat at the foot."
chunks.title: Watson hint 2

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Compare Mr. Mills's claim that he never left his chair with the service record at 9:02, Miss Clarke's account, and his telegram of Thursday."
chunks.title: Watson hint 3
